per_question.question: My mother lives in an adult care home (assisted living). Can she receive Personal Care Services through NC Medicaid while living there?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes—NC Medicaid can cover Personal Care Services for someone living in an adult care home, but only if she meets the congregate-setting PCS eligibility rules. An eligible beneficiary must have a medical, mental, physical, or cognitive condition causing unmet needs with qualifying activities of daily living, and must live in a North Carolina-licensed adult care home, combination home, or certain licensed group homes. `[Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)`

More specifically, Medicaid covers PCS in a congregate setting when the beneficiary needs at least: three of five qualifying ADLs with limited hands-on assistance, or two ADLs with one requiring extensive assistance, or two ADLs with one requiring full dependence assistance. `[Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)`

The policy also requires, among other things, that no other third-party payer be responsible for the PCS, that no family/household member or other informal caregiver is available, willing, and able to provide the authorized services at those times, that the beneficiary be under a physician’s ongoing direct care for the condition causing the functional limits, and that the beneficiary be medically stable and not need continuous nursing care, monitoring, or supervision by a licensed professional. `[Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)`

If she qualifies, the covered PCS can include hands-on help with ADLs, cueing/prompting as part of that hands-on help, certain related IADL assistance, medication assistance tied to the documented condition, help with adaptive devices or durable medical equipment related to qualifying ADLs, and certain special assistance tasks. `[Policy 3L-1 § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)`

But Medicaid does not cover room and board in the adult care home under PCS, and it also does not cover items such as transportation, errands, companion sitting, respite care, or skilled nursing services under this PCS policy. `[Policy 3L-1 § 4.2.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)`

The policy document in the corpus is marked as amended January 1, 2026. `[Policy 3L-1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)`

If you want, I can next help with the practical question: whether your mother’s specific needs sound likely to meet the ADL standard under this policy.

Reason: Congregate PCS beneficiary and facility criteria section from the preferred document.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings when the beneficiary meets the following specific criteria and other items in this section:
has a medical or mental condition, disability, or cognitive impairment and demonstrates unmet needs for, at a minimum:
three of the five qualifying activities of daily living (ADLs) with limited hands-on assistance. Refer to Subsection 5.4.3;
two ADLs, one of which requires extensive assistance; or
two ADLs, one of which requires assistance at the full dependence level.
resides in:
a congregate facility licensed by the State of North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH) as defined in NC G.S. §131D-2.1, a combination home as defined in NC G.S. § 131E-101; or
a group home licensed under Chapter 122C of the General Statutes and under 10A NCAC 27G .5601 (b)(2) as a supervised living facility for two or more adults whose primary diagnosis is mental illness, a developmental disability, or substance abuse dependency and is eligible to receive personal care services under the Medicaid State Plan.
In addition to the specific criteria in Subsection 3.2.1 a and b of this policy, the following criteria must be met:
The congregate setting is safe and free of health hazards for the beneficiary and PCS provider(s), as determined by a facility environmental assessment conducted by NC Medicaid or a DHHS designated contractor;
The congregate setting has received inspection conducted by the Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR)
The place of service is safe for the beneficiary to receive PCS and for an aide to provide PCS;
No other third-party payer is responsible for covering PCS;
No family or household member or other informal caregiver is available, willing, and able to provide the authorized services during those periods of time when the services are provided;
The required PCS are directly linked to a documented medical or mental condition or physical or cognitive impairment causing the functional limitations requiring the PCS;
The beneficiary is under the ongoing direct care of a physician for the medical condition or diagnosis causing the functional limitations; and
The beneficiary is medically stable and does not require continuous care, monitoring (precautionary observation), or supervision (observation resulting in an intervention) by a licensed nurse or other licensed health care professional; and
Screening for Serious Mental Illness (SMI) in Adult Care Homes licensed under G.S. §131D-2.4 Effective November 1, 2018, any Medicaid beneficiary referred to or seeking admission to Adult Care Homes licensed under G.S. 131D-2.4 must be referred to a Tailored Plan Transition Coordinator for the Referral Screening Verification Process. Adult Care Home providers licensed under G.S. § 131D-2.4 shall not receive a PCS assessment or prior approval without verification of a Referral Screening ID.

per_question.question: Can CAP/DA pay to modify a participant's home, and what documentation does the Multidisciplinary Team have to provide for a home modification request?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. CAP/DA can pay for home modifications as part of its “equipment, modification and technology” service when the modification is identified through the comprehensive assessment and is intended to improve the beneficiary’s mobility, safety, independence, community integration, environmental accessibility, or 24/7 coverage needs. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.4.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) [Policy 3K-2 § 5.8.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

Home modifications are specifically allowed only for a beneficiary’s primary private residence owned by the beneficiary or family, for a rented residence when the modifications are portable, or for a rented residence when the owner allows the modification. [Policy 3K-2 § 5.8.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

Covered examples include ramps, grab bars, widening doorways or passages, emergency egress when medically necessary, bathroom modifications, bedroom modifications, kitchen accessibility modifications, and certain other safety or accessibility adaptations. [Policy 3K-2 § 5.8.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

CAP/DA limits equipment, modification, and technology services to $28,000 over the waiver approval cycle, excludes items not of direct medical or remedial benefit, and does not cover items available through DME, orthotics/prosthetics, home health supplies, or EPSDT merely because those programs denied them for lack of medical necessity. [Policy 3K-2 § 5.8.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) [Policy 3K-2 Change Notice 2025-09-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## MDT documentation required for a home modification request

For a home modification request, the multidisciplinary team must provide an assessment of need recommending the modification, and that assessment must include a PT, OT, rehabilitation engineer, or assistive technology professional for ECUs/EADLs certifying necessity. A copy of that assessment must be submitted with the request. [Policy 3K-2 § 5.8.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

When applicable, the request must also include a physician’s signed order certifying that the requested equipment, technology, adaptation, or modification is necessary. [Policy 3K-2 § 5.8.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

When feasible, the request must include up to two competitive quotes for home modifications so the most efficient method can be selected. [Policy 3K-2 § 5.8.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

The required approval and reimbursement documentation also includes a comprehensive multidisciplinary declaration-of-need assessment completed by the case manager identifying the needed equipment, supply, adaptation, or modification; a copy of the physician’s order when applicable; a recommendation by an appropriate professional identifying the beneficiary’s need for the requested modification; the estimated life of the item and how long the beneficiary is expected to benefit from it; and an invoice from the supplier showing the date provided, cost, and related charges, maintained in the CAP Business system. [Policy 3K-2 § 5.8.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

The policy currently in force is the September 1, 2025 revision of Policy 3K-2, which amended all sections and attachments, including Appendix B changes affecting equipment, modification, and technology service limits. [Policy 3K-2 Change Notice 2025-09-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

If you want, I can also turn this into a short checklist the CME/MDT can use for submitting a home modification request.

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave per year can a nursing facility resident take under NC Medicaid, and what conditions apply to that leave?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under the NC Medicaid therapeutic-leave rule surfaced here, a resident may take up to 45 days of therapeutic leave in any calendar year from a Level II, Level III, or Level IV Residential Facility bed, and therapeutic leave is also limited to no more than 15 days within one calendar quarter (three months).

The leave must be for therapeutic purposes only and must be agreed upon by the beneficiary’s treatment team.

The need for the leave, the expectations for the leave, and the therapeutic justification for each instance must be documented in the treatment/habilitation plan and in the beneficiary’s record.

“Therapeutic leave” means an overnight absence from the residential facility, with an expectation of return, to participate in a medically acceptable therapeutic or rehabilitative facility as agreed upon by the treatment team and documented on the treatment/habilitation plan.

A facility must reserve the resident’s bed during approved therapeutic leave and is reimbursed at its full current Medicaid bed rate for that bed during the period of absence, but not for therapeutic leave days that exceed the legal limit.

No more than five consecutive days may be taken without approval of the beneficiary’s treatment team.

The facility must keep a cumulative record of therapeutic-leave days for each beneficiary, note therapeutic leave on the facility’s midnight census, and bill approved leave days as regular residence days.

Therapeutic leave is not applicable if the absence is for inpatient services or any other Medicaid-covered service in the current facility or another facility, and it cannot be paid when Medicaid is paying for any other 24-hour service.

[wrong source: The federal nursing-facility statute requires services to be furnished under a written plan of care designed to meet the resident’s medical, nursing, and psychosocial needs, which helps explain why NC Medicaid ties therapeutic leave to treatment-team approval and plan documentation. [SSA § 1919](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)]

One caution: the section retrieved here is from Policy 8D-2 Residential Treatment Services, not a separate NC nursing-facility manual section, so I could not verify from the surfaced documents alone whether NC Medicaid uses a different therapeutic-leave rule for other categories of nursing-facility residents.

---

Primary sections:
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:8D-2:5.3.1
Title: 5.3.1 Therapeutic Leave
Section: 5.3.1
Policy: 8D-2
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [8D-2, Residential Treatment Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8d-2-residential-treatment-services/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched cover.
Content:
Each Medicaid eligible beneficiary who is occupying a Level II, Level III, or Level IV Residential Facility bed for which the North Carolina Medicaid Program is then paying reimbursement shall be entitled to take up to 45 days of therapeutic leave in any calendar year from any such bed without the facility in which the bed is located suffering any loss of reimbursement during the period of leave. Therapeutic leave is also limited to no more than 15 days within one calendar quarter (three months).
The taking of such leave must be for therapeutic purposes only and must be agreed upon by the beneficiary's treatment team. The necessity for such leave and the expectations involved in such leave shall be documented in the beneficiary's treatment/habilitation plan and the therapeutic justification for
each instance of such leave entered into the beneficiary's record maintained at the Residential Facility's site.
Therapeutic leave shall be defined as the absence of a beneficiary from the residential facility overnight, with the expectation of return, to participate in a medically acceptable therapeutic or rehabilitative facility as agreed upon by the treatment team and documented on the treatment/habilitation plan.
Facilities must reserve a therapeutically absent beneficiary's bed for him and are prohibited from deriving any Medicaid revenue for that beneficiary other than the reimbursement for that bed during the period of absence. Facilities shall be reimbursed at their full current Medicaid bed rate for a bed reserved due to therapeutic leave. Facilities shall not be reimbursed for therapeutic leave days taken which exceed the legal limit.
No more than five consecutive days may be taken without the approval of the beneficiary's treatment team.
Facilities must keep a cumulative record of therapeutic leave days taken by each beneficiary for reference and audit purposes. In addition, beneficiaries on therapeutic leave must be noted as such on the facility's midnight census. Facilities shall bill Medicaid for approved therapeutic leave days as regular residence days.
The official record of therapeutic leave days taken for each patient shall be maintained by the State or its agent.
Therapeutic leave is not applicable in cases when the therapeutic leave is for the purpose of receiving inpatient services or any other Medicaid covered service in the facility of current residence or in another facility. Therapeutic leave cannot be paid when Medicaid is paying for any other 24-hour service.
Transportation from a facility to the site of therapeutic leave is not considered to be an emergency; therefore, ambulance service for this purpose shall not be reimbursed by Medicaid. Medicaid shall not cover nonemergency medical transportation.

ID: sec:doc:federal_statute:ssa-title-19:1919
Title: Section 1919. Requirements for nursing facilities
Section: 1919
Policy: SSA-Title-19
Type: federal_statute
Citation link: [Social Security Act — Title XIX (Medicaid)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)
Reason: Matched cover.
Content:
(a) "Nursing facility" defined

In this subchapter, the term "nursing facility" means an institution (or a distinct part of an institution) which—

(1) is primarily engaged in providing to residents—

(A) skilled nursing care and related services for residents who require medical or nursing care,

(B) rehabilitation services for the rehabilitation of injured, disabled, or sick persons, or

(C) on a regular basis, health-related care and services to individuals who because of their mental or physical condition require care and services (above the level of room and board) which can be made available to them only through institutional facilities,

and is not primarily for the care and treatment of mental diseases;

(2) has in effect a transfer agreement (meeting the requirements of section 1395x(l) of this title) with one or more hospitals having agreements in effect under section 1395cc of this title; and

(3) meets the requirements for a nursing facility described in subsections (b), (c), and (d) of this section.

Such term also includes any facility which is located in a State on an Indian reservation and is certified by the Secretary as meeting the requirements of paragraph (1) and subsections (b), (c), and (d).

(b) Requirements relating to provision of services

(1) Quality of life

(A) In general

A nursing facility must care for its residents in such a manner and in such an environment as will promote maintenance or enhancement of the quality of life of each resident.

(B) Quality assessment and assurance

A nursing facility must maintain a quality assessment and assurance committee, consisting of the director of nursing services, a physician designated by the facility, and at least 3 other members of the facility's staff, which (i) meets at least quarterly to identify issues with respect to which quality assessment and assurance activities are necessary and (ii) develops and implements appropriate plans of action to correct identified quality deficiencies. A State or the Secretary may not require disclosure of the records of such committee except insofar as such disclosure is related to the compliance of such committee with the requirements of this subparagraph.

(2) Scope of services and activities under plan of care

A nursing facility must provide services and activities to attain or maintain the highest practicable physical, mental, and psychosocial well-being of each resident in accordance with a written plan of care which—

(A) describes the medical, nursing, and psychosocial needs of the resident and how such needs will be met;

(B) is initially prepared, with the participation to the extent practicable of the resident or the resident's family or legal representative, by a team which includes the resident's attending physician and a registered professional nurse with responsibility for the resident; and

(C) is periodically reviewed and revised by such team after each assessment under paragraph (3).

(3) Residents' assessment

(A) Requirement

A nursing facility must conduct a comprehensive, accurate, standardized, reproducible assessment of each resident's functional capacity, which assessment—

(i) describes the resident's capability to perform daily life functions and significant impairments in functional capacity;

(ii) is based on a uniform minimum data set specified by the Secretary under subsection (f)(6)(A);

(iii) uses an instrument which is specified by the State under subsection (e)(5); and

(iv) includes the identification of medical problems.

(B) Certification

(i) In general

Each such assessment must be conducted or coordinated (with the appropriate participation of health professionals) by a registered professional nurse who signs and certifies the completion of the assessment. Each individual who completes a portion of such an assessment shall sign and certify as to the accuracy of that portion of the assessment.

(ii) Penalty for falsification

(I) An individual who willfully and knowingly certifies under clause (i) a material and false statement in a resident assessment is subject to a civil money penalty of not more than $1,000 with respect to each assessment.

(II) An individual who willfully and knowingly causes another individual to certify under clause (i) a material and false statement in a resident assessment is subject to a civil money penalty of not more than $5,000 with respect to each assessment.

(III) The provisions of section 1320a–7a of this title (other than subsections (a) and (b)) shall apply to a civil money penalty under this clause in the same manner as such provisions apply to a penalty or proceeding under section 1320a–7a(a) of this title.

(iii) Use of independent assessors

If a State determines, under a survey under subsection (g) or otherwise, that there has been a knowing and willful certification of false assessments under this paragraph, the State may require (for a period specified by the State) that resident assessments under this paragraph be conducted and certified by individuals who are independent of the facility and who are approved by the State.

(C) Frequency

(i) In general

Such an assessment must be conducted—

(I) promptly upon (but no later than 14 days after the date of) admission for each individual admitted on or after October 1, 1990, and by not later than October 1, 1991, for each resident of the facility on that date;

(II) promptly after a significant change in the resident's physical or mental condition; and

(III) in no case less often than once every 12 months.

(ii) Resident review

The nursing facility must examine each resident no less frequently than once every 3 months and, as appropriate, revise the resident's assessment to assure the continuing accuracy of the assessment.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:8D-2:5.3.1
Title: 5.3.1 Therapeutic Leave
Section: 5.3.1
Policy: 8D-2
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2025-01-01
Citation link: [8D-2, Residential Treatment Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8d-2-residential-treatment-services/download?attachment)

Content:
Each Medicaid eligible beneficiary who is occupying a Level II, Level III, or Level IV Residential Facility bed for which the North Carolina Medicaid Program is then paying reimbursement shall be entitled to take up to 45 days of therapeutic leave in any calendar year from any such bed without the facility in which the bed is located suffering any loss of reimbursement during the period of leave. Therapeutic leave is also limited to no more than 15 days within one calendar quarter (three months).
The taking of such leave must be for therapeutic purposes only and must be agreed upon by the beneficiary's treatment team. The necessity for such leave and the expectations involved in such leave shall be documented in the beneficiary's treatment/habilitation plan and the therapeutic justification for
each instance of such leave entered into the beneficiary's record maintained at the Residential Facility's site.
Therapeutic leave shall be defined as the absence of a beneficiary from the residential facility overnight, with the expectation of return, to participate in a medically acceptable therapeutic or rehabilitative facility as agreed upon by the treatment team and documented on the treatment/habilitation plan.
Facilities must reserve a therapeutically absent beneficiary's bed for him and are prohibited from deriving any Medicaid revenue for that beneficiary other than the reimbursement for that bed during the period of absence. Facilities shall be reimbursed at their full current Medicaid bed rate for a bed reserved due to therapeutic leave. Facilities shall not be reimbursed for therapeutic leave days taken which exceed the legal limit.
No more than five consecutive days may be taken without the approval of the beneficiary's treatment team.
Facilities must keep a cumulative record of therapeutic leave days taken by each beneficiary for reference and audit purposes. In addition, beneficiaries on therapeutic leave must be noted as such on the facility's midnight census. Facilities shall bill Medicaid for approved therapeutic leave days as regular residence days.
The official record of therapeutic leave days taken for each patient shall be maintained by the State or its agent.
Therapeutic leave is not applicable in cases when the therapeutic leave is for the purpose of receiving inpatient services or any other Medicaid covered service in the facility of current residence or in another facility. Therapeutic leave cannot be paid when Medicaid is paying for any other 24-hour service.
Transportation from a facility to the site of therapeutic leave is not considered to be an emergency; therefore, ambulance service for this purpose shall not be reimbursed by Medicaid. Medicaid shall not cover nonemergency medical transportation.

Title: Section 1919. Requirements for nursing facilities
Section: 1919
Policy: SSA-Title-19
Type: federal_statute
Citation link: [Social Security Act — Title XIX (Medicaid)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)

Content:
(a) "Nursing facility" defined

In this subchapter, the term "nursing facility" means an institution (or a distinct part of an institution) which—

(1) is primarily engaged in providing to residents—

(A) skilled nursing care and related services for residents who require medical or nursing care,

(B) rehabilitation services for the rehabilitation of injured, disabled, or sick persons, or

(C) on a regular basis, health-related care and services to individuals who because of their mental or physical condition require care and services (above the level of room and board) which can be made available to them only through institutional facilities,

and is not primarily for the care and treatment of mental diseases;

(2) has in effect a transfer agreement (meeting the requirements of section 1395x(l) of this title) with one or more hospitals having agreements in effect under section 1395cc of this title; and

(3) meets the requirements for a nursing facility described in subsections (b), (c), and (d) of this section.

Such term also includes any facility which is located in a State on an Indian reservation and is certified by the Secretary as meeting the requirements of paragraph (1) and subsections (b), (c), and (d).

(b) Requirements relating to provision of services

(1) Quality of life

(A) In general

A nursing facility must care for its residents in such a manner and in such an environment as will promote maintenance or enhancement of the quality of life of each resident.

(B) Quality assessment and assurance

A nursing facility must maintain a quality assessment and assurance committee, consisting of the director of nursing services, a physician designated by the facility, and at least 3 other members of the facility's staff, which (i) meets at least quarterly to identify issues with respect to which quality assessment and assurance activities are necessary and (ii) develops and implements appropriate plans of action to correct identified quality deficiencies. A State or the Secretary may not require disclosure of the records of such committee except insofar as such disclosure is related to the compliance of such committee with the requirements of this subparagraph.

(2) Scope of services and activities under plan of care

A nursing facility must provide services and activities to attain or maintain the highest practicable physical, mental, and psychosocial well-being of each resident in accordance with a written plan of care which—

(A) describes the medical, nursing, and psychosocial needs of the resident and how such needs will be met;

(B) is initially prepared, with the participation to the extent practicable of the resident or the resident's family or legal representative, by a team which includes the resident's attending physician and a registered professional nurse with responsibility for the resident; and

(C) is periodically reviewed and revised by such team after each assessment under paragraph (3).

(3) Residents' assessment

(A) Requirement

A nursing facility must conduct a comprehensive, accurate, standardized, reproducible assessment of each resident's functional capacity, which assessment—

(i) describes the resident's capability to perform daily life functions and significant impairments in functional capacity;

(ii) is based on a uniform minimum data set specified by the Secretary under subsection (f)(6)(A);

(iii) uses an instrument which is specified by the State under subsection (e)(5); and

(iv) includes the identification of medical problems.

(B) Certification

(i) In general

Each such assessment must be conducted or coordinated (with the appropriate participation of health professionals) by a registered professional nurse who signs and certifies the completion of the assessment. Each individual who completes a portion of such an assessment shall sign and certify as to the accuracy of that portion of the assessment.

(ii) Penalty for falsification

(I) An individual who willfully and knowingly certifies under clause (i) a material and false statement in a resident assessment is subject to a civil money penalty of not more than $1,000 with respect to each assessment.

(II) An individual who willfully and knowingly causes another individual to certify under clause (i) a material and false statement in a resident assessment is subject to a civil money penalty of not more than $5,000 with respect to each assessment.

(III) The provisions of section 1320a–7a of this title (other than subsections (a) and (b)) shall apply to a civil money penalty under this clause in the same manner as such provisions apply to a penalty or proceeding under section 1320a–7a(a) of this title.

(iii) Use of independent assessors

If a State determines, under a survey under subsection (g) or otherwise, that there has been a knowing and willful certification of false assessments under this paragraph, the State may require (for a period specified by the State) that resident assessments under this paragraph be conducted and certified by individuals who are independent of the facility and who are approved by the State.

(C) Frequency

(i) In general

Such an assessment must be conducted—

(I) promptly upon (but no later than 14 days after the date of) admission for each individual admitted on or after October 1, 1990, and by not later than October 1, 1991, for each resident of the facility on that date;

(II) promptly after a significant change in the resident's physical or mental condition; and

(III) in no case less often than once every 12 months.

(ii) Resident review

The nursing facility must examine each resident no less frequently than once every 3 months and, as appropriate, revise the resident's assessment to assure the continuing accuracy of the assessment.

(D) Use

The results of such an assessment shall be used in developing, reviewing, and revising the resident's plan of care under paragraph (2).

per_question.question: What notice is a Private Duty Nursing provider required to give before it stops serving a Medicaid beneficiary?
per_question.agent_answer:
A Private Duty Nursing provider is not given a beneficiary-advance-notice period in the PDN clinical policy section I retrieved. Instead, the policy requires notice to **NC Medicaid** after termination/discharge events. For beneficiaries **21 and older**, if the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary, the provider must submit the **DMA-3513 PDN Discharge Summary Form** to NC Medicaid **within five business days**. If the discharge is because another source of nursing coverage is available, the provider must notify NC Medicaid and submit the DMA-3513 within **five business days**, including the **last date PDN services were provided and billable to Medicaid** and the **name of the other coverage source**. If the attending physician discharges the beneficiary, the provider must send NC Medicaid the physician’s order to terminate services and the DMA-3513 within **five business days**. [Policy 3G-1 § 5.2.4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)

For beneficiaries **under 21**, the policy likewise requires notice to **NC Medicaid**, not a stated advance notice to the beneficiary. If the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary, the provider must send a copy of the **physician’s order to terminate services** to NC Medicaid within **five business days**. If the discharge is because another source of nursing coverage exists, the provider must notify NC Medicaid in writing and report the **last date PDN services were provided and billable to Medicaid** and the **name of the other source of coverage**. If the attending physician discharges the beneficiary, the provider must provide NC Medicaid the physician’s order within **five business days**. [Policy 3G-2 § 5.2.4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-2-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-under-21-years-age/download?attachment)

So, based on the PDN policies I could verify, the required notice is a **post-discharge notice to NC Medicaid within five business days** in the termination situations described above, rather than a specified advance notice period to the beneficiary. [Policy 3G-1 § 5.2.4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment) [Policy 3G-2 § 5.2.4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-2-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-under-21-years-age/download?attachment)

If you want, I can also check whether a separate home care licensing rule, provider participation agreement, or due-process rule imposes a **beneficiary advance notice** requirement outside the PDN clinical coverage policies.

scores.explanation: The agent's answer accurately captures all key facts from the reference and evidence: the DMA-3513 form requirement, the 5 business day deadline, the notification to NC Medicaid (not advance notice to beneficiary), the requirement to include last date of billable services and name of other coverage source when discharging due to alternative coverage, and the physician discharge scenario. The agent goes beyond the reference by also covering Policy 3G-2 (under-21 beneficiaries), which is supported by the evidence block. No hallucinations are present - all claims are directly supported by the evidence. Citations are precise, referencing specific section numbers (5.2.4.1) and both policy documents (3G-1 and 3G-2) with direct URLs. The agent also helpfully clarifies that the notice requirement runs to NC Medicaid rather than to the beneficiary, which is an accurate and useful distinction. The offer to check additional sources for beneficiary advance notice requirements shows appropriate epistemic humility.

Title: Section 1919. Requirements for nursing facilities
Section: 1919
Policy: SSA-Title-19
Type: federal_statute
Citation link: [Social Security Act — Title XIX (Medicaid)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)
Reason: Matched notice.
Content:
(a) "Nursing facility" defined

In this subchapter, the term "nursing facility" means an institution (or a distinct part of an institution) which—

(1) is primarily engaged in providing to residents—

(A) skilled nursing care and related services for residents who require medical or nursing care,

(B) rehabilitation services for the rehabilitation of injured, disabled, or sick persons, or

(C) on a regular basis, health-related care and services to individuals who because of their mental or physical condition require care and services (above the level of room and board) which can be made available to them only through institutional facilities,

and is not primarily for the care and treatment of mental diseases;

(2) has in effect a transfer agreement (meeting the requirements of section 1395x(l) of this title) with one or more hospitals having agreements in effect under section 1395cc of this title; and

(3) meets the requirements for a nursing facility described in subsections (b), (c), and (d) of this section.

Such term also includes any facility which is located in a State on an Indian reservation and is certified by the Secretary as meeting the requirements of paragraph (1) and subsections (b), (c), and (d).

(b) Requirements relating to provision of services

(1) Quality of life

(A) In general

A nursing facility must care for its residents in such a manner and in such an environment as will promote maintenance or enhancement of the quality of life of each resident.

(B) Quality assessment and assurance

A nursing facility must maintain a quality assessment and assurance committee, consisting of the director of nursing services, a physician designated by the facility, and at least 3 other members of the facility's staff, which (i) meets at least quarterly to identify issues with respect to which quality assessment and assurance activities are necessary and (ii) develops and implements appropriate plans of action to correct identified quality deficiencies. A State or the Secretary may not require disclosure of the records of such committee except insofar as such disclosure is related to the compliance of such committee with the requirements of this subparagraph.

(2) Scope of services and activities under plan of care

A nursing facility must provide services and activities to attain or maintain the highest practicable physical, mental, and psychosocial well-being of each resident in accordance with a written plan of care which—

(A) describes the medical, nursing, and psychosocial needs of the resident and how such needs will be met;

(B) is initially prepared, with the participation to the extent practicable of the resident or the resident's family or legal representative, by a team which includes the resident's attending physician and a registered professional nurse with responsibility for the resident; and

(C) is periodically reviewed and revised by such team after each assessment under paragraph (3).

(3) Residents' assessment

(A) Requirement

A nursing facility must conduct a comprehensive, accurate, standardized, reproducible assessment of each resident's functional capacity, which assessment—

(i) describes the resident's capability to perform daily life functions and significant impairments in functional capacity;

(ii) is based on a uniform minimum data set specified by the Secretary under subsection (f)(6)(A);

(iii) uses an instrument which is specified by the State under subsection (e)(5); and

(iv) includes the identification of medical problems.

(B) Certification

(i) In general

Each such assessment must be conducted or coordinated (with the appropriate participation of health professionals) by a registered professional nurse who signs and certifies the completion of the assessment. Each individual who completes a portion of such an assessment shall sign and certify as to the accuracy of that portion of the assessment.

(ii) Penalty for falsification

(I) An individual who willfully and knowingly certifies under clause (i) a material and false statement in a resident assessment is subject to a civil money penalty of not more than $1,000 with respect to each assessment.

(II) An individual who willfully and knowingly causes another individual to certify under clause (i) a material and false statement in a resident assessment is subject to a civil money penalty of not more than $5,000 with respect to each assessment.

(III) The provisions of section 1320a–7a of this title (other than subsections (a) and (b)) shall apply to a civil money penalty under this clause in the same manner as such provisions apply to a penalty or proceeding under section 1320a–7a(a) of this title.

(iii) Use of independent assessors

If a State determines, under a survey under subsection (g) or otherwise, that there has been a knowing and willful certification of false assessments under this paragraph, the State may require (for a period specified by the State) that resident assessments under this paragraph be conducted and certified by individuals who are independent of the facility and who are approved by the State.

(C) Frequency

(i) In general

Such an assessment must be conducted—

(I) promptly upon (but no later than 14 days after the date of) admission for each individual admitted on or after October 1, 1990, and by not later than October 1, 1991, for each resident of the facility on that date;

(II) promptly after a significant change in the resident's physical or mental condition; and

(III) in no case less often than once every 12 months.

(ii) Resident review

The nursing facility must examine each resident no less frequently than once every 3 months and, as appropriate, revise the resident's assessment to assure the continuing accuracy of the assessment.

(D) Use

The results of such an assessment shall be used in developing, reviewing, and revising the resident's plan of care under paragraph (2).

ID: sec:doc:state_plan_amendment:SPA 23-0050:_s2
Title: 8. Private Duty Nursing Services
Policy: SPA 23-0050
Type: state_plan_amendment
Citation link: [SPA 23-0050 Proposed Amendment Sent to CMS (Private Duty Nursing (PDN)-Addition of Near Relative)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/spa-23-0050-proposed-amendment-sent-cms-private-duty-nursing-pdn-addition-near-relative/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched not covered.
Content:
Medically necessary private duty nursing (PDN) services are provided under the direction of the recipient's physician in accordance with 42 CFR 440.80 and prior approval by the Division of Medical Assistance, or its designee.
Residents who are in adult care homes are not eligible for this service. This exclusion does not violate comparability requirements as adult care home residents do not have the medical necessity for continuous nursing care. According to State regulations for adult care homes, people are not to be admitted for professional nursing care under continuous medical supervision and residents who develop a need for such care are to be placed elsewhere. In addition, recipients in hospitals, nursing facilities, intermediate care facilities for the mentally retarded, rehabilitation centers, and other institutional settings are not eligible for this service. PDN services are not covered while an individual is being observed or treated in a hospital emergency room or similar environment.
This service is only approvable based on the need for PDN services in the patient's private residence. An individual with a medical condition that necessitates this service normally is unable to leave the home without being accompanied by a licensed nurse and leaving the home requires considerable and taxing effort. An individual may utilize the approved hours of coverage outside of his/her residence during those hours when the individual's normal life activities take the patient out of the home. The need for nursing care to participate in activities outside of the home is not a basis for authorizing PDN services or expanding the hours needed for PDN services.
Medicaid will not reimburse for Personal Care Services, Skilled Nursing Visits, or Home Health Aide Services provided during the same hours of the day as PDN services.
Medicaid Payments for PDN are made only to agencies enrolled with the Division of Medical Assistance as providers for the service. An enrolled provider must be a State licensed home care agency within North Carolina that is approved in its license to provide nursing services within the State. PDN services shall be rendered by a licensed registered nurse (RN) or licensed practical nurse (LPN) who is licensed by the North Carolina Board of Nursing and employed by a licensed home care agency.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3G-1:5.2.2.5
Title: 5.2.2.5 Reauthorization Process and Documentation Requirements
Section: 5.2.2.5
Policy: 3G-1
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched documentation.
Content:
To recertify for PDN services, the PDN service provider shall enter a request for reauthorization and submit the following required documents to NC Medicaid at least 15 business days prior to the end of the current approved PA period:
A copy of the CMS-485 (Home Health Certification and Plan of Care Form) signed and dated by the attending physician;
DMA-3509 (PDN Medical Update Form);
Nursing notes from the last authorization period. At least five (5) nonconsecutive calendar days are required;
Private health insurance coverage or denial documentation for current approval period, if applicable;
Missed shift hours report during the previous 180-day authorization period.
The PA period is a maximum of 180 days. The attending physician-signed CMS-485 (Home Health Certification and Plan of Care Form) and DMA-3509 (PDN Medical Update Form) shall be uploaded every 60 days. A verbal order and date signed by RN if CMS-485 (Locator 23) is not signed by the attending physician in advance of the certification period is acceptable. All attending physician signed 485's for the 180-day certification period shall be uploaded before the PA expiration date:
By PA day 60: DMA-3509 (PDN Medical Update Form) and attending physician-signed CMS-485 (Home Health Certification and Plan of Care Form) shall be submitted.
By PA day 120: DMA-3509 (PDN Medical Update Form) and attending physician-signed CMS-485 (Home Health Certification and Plan of Care Form) shall be submitted.
PDN service provider(s) shall disclose the total number of missed shift hours during the previous 180-day authorization period, on the DMA-3509 (PDN Medical Update form), with an attestation that this report accurately reflects the missed shift hours and shall be provided to the beneficiary or legal guardian upon request.
At NC Medicaid's discretion, an in-home assessment may be performed by NC Medicaid or its designee. NC Medicaid reserves the right to request additional records, including hospitalization records and discharge summary, medical records from attending physician or medical specialists, and any other medical records.
NC Medicaid reserves the right to verify caregiver's employment schedule annually and as deemed appropriate by NC Medicaid.
Note: Once all required documentation is received, NC Medicaid shall conduct the clinical review for reauthorization. Incomplete or omitted documentation or a request for additional information not received within the specified timeframe, is handled as an incomplete request and may result in denial of the PA request.
If the request for reauthorization is received after the beginning of the new authorization period, NC Medicaid shall only consider approval of PA from the date of request submission.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3G-1:5.2.4.1
Title: 5.2.4.1 Notification of Termination
Section: 5.2.4.1
Policy: 3G-1
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)

Content:
The termination process is determined by the following:
If the PDN service provider discharges the beneficiary, this service provider shall submit the DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form) to NC Medicaid within five (5) business days.
If the PDN service provider discharges the beneficiary from Medicaid coverage because there is another source of nursing care coverage, this provider shall notify NC Medicaid and submit the DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form) within five (5) business days The notification shall include the last date that PDN services were provided
and can be billed to Medicaid and the name of the other source of coverage.
If the attending physician discharges the beneficiary, this PDN service provider shall provide to NC Medicaid, within five (5) business days, the attending physician's order to terminate PDN services and the DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form). The decision of the beneficiary's attending physician and/or the PDN service provider to discharge the beneficiary cannot be appealed to NC Medicaid.
If services are terminated as a result of the beneficiary's loss of NC Medicaid eligibility, or if no PDN services are provided during the 30 consecutive days for any reason including hospitalization, then the prior approval process shall be initiated again as outlined in Subsections 5.1 and 5.2.
PDN service providers shall notify NC Medicaid when a beneficiary is hospitalized for 30 days or greater.
NC Medicaid shall terminate PDN if a review of services shows NC Medicaid eligibility, policy criteria and/or medical necessity is not met. NC Medicaid of its designee shall provide notice of an adverse decision in writing to the beneficiary/legal representative that includes information about appeal rights.
Note: PDN service provider(s) shall disclose the final number of missed shift hours during the authorization period, on the DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form), with an attestation that this report accurately reflects the missed shift hours and shall be provided to the beneficiary or legal guardian upon request.

Content:
The termination process is determined by the following:
If the PDN service provider discharges the beneficiary, the service provider shall send a copy of the physician's order to terminate services to NC Medicaid within five (5) business days.
If the PDN service provider discharges the beneficiary from Medicaid coverage because there is another source of nursing care coverage, the service provider shall notify NC Medicaid in writing. The notification must report the last date that PDN services were provided and can be billed to Medicaid and the name of the other source of coverage as applicable.
If the attending physician discharges the beneficiary, the PDN service provider shall provide NC Medicaid, within five (5) business days, the physician's order to terminate beneficiary services.
If services are terminated as a result of the beneficiary's loss of Medicaid, or if no PDN services are provided during the 30 consecutive days for any reason such as a hospitalization, then the prior approval process must be initiated once again as outlined in Subsections 5.1 and 5.2. PDN service providers shall notify NC Medicaid when a beneficiary is hospitalized.
Note: The decision of the beneficiary's attending physician and/or the PDN service provider to discharge the beneficiary cannot be appealed to NC Medicaid.

per_question.question: When will NC Medicaid refuse to pay for an ambulance trip — which ambulance transports are excluded from coverage?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid will refuse payment for an ambulance trip when the trip does not meet the policy’s coverage criteria, when required prior approval was not obtained for certain out-of-state non-emergency transports, or when the transport falls into one of the policy’s expressly non-covered categories. [Policy 15 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) [Policy 15 § 5.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

## Main exclusions and non-covered ambulance situations

NC Medicaid covers ambulance services for emergencies only to the extent needed to screen and stabilize the beneficiary, and payment for emergency claims is based on retrospective review of the beneficiary’s presenting history and symptoms. [Policy 15 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) If that review shows the trip did not meet the emergency coverage standard, payment may be denied. [Policy 15 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

For non-emergency ambulance service, prior approval is required for ground or air transport from North Carolina to another state, from one state to another, or from another state back to North Carolina, and that approval must be obtained before the service is rendered. [Policy 15 § 5.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) The policy also states that getting prior approval does not itself guarantee payment, because the beneficiary still must be Medicaid-eligible on the date of service and the service still must be appropriate and medically necessary. [Policy 15 § 5.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

NC Medicaid expressly lists these ambulance situations as non-covered:
- when an ambulance is called and no treatment is needed; [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- when the ambulance responds to a false alarm call; [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- when the beneficiary refuses all medical services; [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- when the ambulance transport is for a medical service that is not a Medicaid covered service; [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- commercial airline tickets; [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- airstrip fees; [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- charges for taxes, including local, state, and federal taxes; [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- separate additional charges for nursing personnel who are employees of a facility or ambulance service; [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- waiting fees; [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- separate billing for oxygen and other items and supplies, because those are included in the base rate and are not separately reimbursable; and [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- services other than those listed in the policy’s covered-services subsection. [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

## Mileage-related limits

For ground ambulance, mileage to a facility that is not the nearest appropriate facility is not covered. [Policy 15 § 1.1.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) In addition, ground ambulance loaded mileage is reimbursable only for out-of-county transport, and in-county loaded ground mileage is not reimbursable. [Policy 15 § 1.1.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

## Documentation-related nonpayment risk

For unscheduled or scheduled non-emergency ambulance trips on a non-repetitive basis, the provider must still meet all coverage criteria, including call report criteria, and the policy says that a signed physician certification statement by itself does not prove medical necessity. [Policy 15 § 7.3.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) That means NC Medicaid can refuse payment even if paperwork exists, if the transport was not actually medically necessary under the policy. [Policy 15 § 7.3.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

## Beneficiaries under 21

For Medicaid beneficiaries under age 21, the policy’s EPSDT section says NC Medicaid must cover services, products, or procedures if they are medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or condition identified through a screening examination. [Policy 15 § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) The policy also says service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location, and other specific criteria may be exceeded or may not apply if the provider’s documentation shows the requested service meets EPSDT criteria. [Policy 15 § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:15:7.3.2
Title: 7.3.2 Non-Emergency Ambulance Services That Are Either Unscheduled or That Are Scheduled on a Non-Repetitive Basis
Section: 7.3.2
Policy: 15
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched cover.
Content:
For a Medicaid beneficiary who is under the care of a physician, the ambulance provider shall obtain a written order certifying the medical necessity from the beneficiary's attending physician within 48 hours after the transport.
If the ambulance provider cannot obtain the written order and certification with appropriate signatures within 21 calendar days following the date of service, the provider shall document the attempts to obtain the requested order and certification and may then submit the claim to NC Medicaid's designee.
If the ambulance provider cannot obtain a signed physician certification statement from the beneficiary's attending physician, he shall obtain a signed certification statement from either the physician assistant (PA), nurse practitioner (NP), clinical nurse specialist (CNS), registered nurse (RN), or discharge planner who has personal knowledge of the beneficiary's condition at the time the ambulance transport is ordered, or the service is furnished.
This individual shall be employed by the beneficiary's attending physician or by the hospital or facility where the beneficiary is being treated and from which the beneficiary is transported.
A physician order is not required for a Medicaid beneficiary who resides at home or in a facility and is not under the direct care of a physician.
The presence of the signed physician certification statement does not necessarily demonstrate that the transport was medically necessary and that it met coverage criteria. The ambulance provider shall meet all coverage criteria, including call report criteria, in order for reimbursement to be made.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:15:5.1
Title: 5.1 Prior Approval
Section: 5.1
Policy: 15
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched cover.
Content:
Prior approval (PA) is required for non-emergency ambulance services for a Medicaid beneficiary by ground or air from North Carolina to another state, from one state to another, or from another state back to North Carolina. Medical necessity determination is based on the documentation submitted by the provider. PA must be obtained before rendering out-of-state non-emergency ambulance services. PA for ambulance service is separate from PA for a medical procedure or treatment provided out of state.
Obtaining PA does not guarantee payment, ensure beneficiary eligibility on the date of service, or guarantee a post-payment review to verify that the service was appropriate and medically necessary. A beneficiary must be eligible for Medicaid coverage on the date the procedure is performed, or the service rendered. Requirements for billing Medicaid beneficiaries are outlined in 10A NCAC 22J.0106 (d).
Services must be provided in compliance with all applicable rules, regulations, laws, and current standards of practice. When requesting authorization for payment of services, the provider shall submit the beneficiary's face sheet and any other relevant information that demonstrates the beneficiary had an emergency medical condition as defined in 42 C.F.R. 489.24(c)(3).
A provider requesting PA for state-to-state ambulance transport shall submit the request by the provider (currently enrolled in NC Medicaid) to the fiscal agent. PA is not required for in-state emergency ambulance services, ground or air, for Medicaid beneficiaries.

Citation link: [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched not covered.
Content:
Loaded mileage is the number of miles for which the beneficiary is transported in the ambulance vehicle.
For air medical ambulance (fixed wing and rotary wing), the point of origin includes the beneficiary's loading point and runway taxiing until the beneficiary is offloaded from the air medical ambulance. Air mileage is based on loaded miles flown, as expressed in statute miles, and is reimbursable.
For ground ambulance, loaded mileage is from the point of origin to the nearest appropriate facility. Mileage to a facility that does not meet this criterion is not covered. Ground ambulance loaded mileage is reimbursable only for out-ofcounty transport. In-county loaded ground mileage is not reimbursable.
Out of county transport is a transport by ambulance in which the final destination of the beneficiary is outside the limits of the county in which the transport originated.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:15:2.2.1
Title: 2.2.1 EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age
Section: 2.2.1
Policy: 15
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
Reason: EPSDT special-provision section that may modify policy limitations for beneficiaries under 21.
Content:
42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination ** (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed clinician).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services will be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:15:3.2.1
Title: 3.2.1 Specific criteria covered by Medicaid
Section: 3.2.1
Policy: 15
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
Reason: Direct coverage-detail section from the preferred document.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover emergency and ambulance services when the beneficiary meets the following specific criteria:
Coverage for emergency services shall be provided to the extent necessary to screen and to stabilize the beneficiary;
shall not require prior authorization of the services if a prudent layperson acting reasonably would have believed that an emergency medical condition existed; and
Payment of claims for emergency services shall be based on the retrospective review of the presenting history and symptoms of the beneficiary.

per_question.question: Will the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy (5B) pay for chiropractic treatment?
per_question.agent_answer:
No. Policy 5B covers **orthotics and prosthetics and related supplies/devices**, not chiropractic treatment. Medicaid covers under Policy 5B only when the item is an orthotic or prosthetic, is medically necessary, and meets the policy’s device-specific coverage requirements. [Policy 5B § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

Policy 5B also says an unlisted request for adults must still be for a **device** that fits the definition of an orthotic or prosthetic; Attachment E does not expand the policy to cover unrelated treatment modalities such as chiropractic care. [Policy 5B Attachment E](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

If a service does not meet the criteria in Section 3.0, Policy 5B says Medicaid does **not** cover the procedure, product, or service related to this policy. [Policy 5B § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

For beneficiaries under 21, Policy 5B includes the EPSDT special provision, which says policy limits may be exceeded for medically necessary services, products, or procedures that meet EPSDT criteria; however, the section retrieved does not specifically state that chiropractic treatment is covered under Policy 5B. [Policy 5B § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

If you want, I can also check whether **chiropractic treatment is covered anywhere else in NC Medicaid**, outside Policy 5B.

scores.explanation: The agent correctly answers 'No' and accurately explains that Policy 5B covers orthotic and prosthetic devices, not chiropractic treatment. The core facts align with the reference answer. However, the agent introduces some minor embellishments: it references '§ 3.2.1' and 'Attachment E' with specific URL citations that appear in the evidence, which is fine, but it frames the answer somewhat awkwardly by discussing what Policy 5B does cover rather than cleanly stating chiropractic is outside the policy's scope entirely. The agent's note about EPSDT (§ 2.2.1) is supported by evidence but adds unnecessary complexity. The agent does not explicitly state the key insight from the reference answer — that chiropractic services never fall within the policy's coverage at all (not merely excluded by § 4.1), and that chiropractic coverage is governed by a different policy. The citation to '§ 3.2.1' is supported by evidence. The agent's framing of § 4.1 as applying to chiropractic is slightly misleading (the reference notes chiropractic never falls within scope, so § 4.1 doesn't even apply), representing a minor factual imprecision. Overall the answer is acceptable but less precise than the reference.

Medicaid covers under Policy 5B only when the item is an orthotic or prosthetic, is medically necessary, and meets the policy’s device-specific coverage requirements.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:5B:Attachment E
Title: Attachment E: Requesting Unlisted Orthotics and Prosthetics for Adults
Section: Attachment E
Policy: 5B
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched cover.
Content:
In compliance with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Home Health Final Rule, 42 CFR Part 440.70, please follow these guidelines when requesting medical necessity reviews for Orthotics and Prosthetics for adults not listed in Attachment B or the O&P fee schedule.
The general requirements and criteria set forth in clinical coverage policy 5B must be met. This includes, but is not limited to:
The device being requested must fit the definition of an orthotic or prosthetic;
The beneficiary must be enrolled in the NC Medicaid program and be eligible for the device;
The provider must be enrolled in the NC Medicaid program with an appropriate taxonomy;
The requested device must be safe, effective, economical and not intended for the convenience of the beneficiary, the beneficiary's caregiver, or the provider;
The device must be medical in nature, generally recognized as an accepted method of treatment, and must not be experimental or investigational;
The device must be ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner;
The device must be medically necessary to maintain or improve a beneficiary's medical, physical or functional level, and appropriate for use in any non-institutional setting in which normal life activities take place;
A documented face-to-face encounter with the beneficiary and the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner related to the primary reason the beneficiary requires the device must have occurred no more than six months prior to the initiation of orthotics and prosthetics; and
The beneficiary's need for the device must be reviewed by the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner at least annually.
If the provider determines that the applicable requirements and criteria set forth in clinical coverage policy 5B have been met, then the provider may submit a completed Certificate of Medical Necessity/Prior Approval (CMN/PA) form and the usual supportive prior authorization documentation through NCTracks for a medical necessity review.
Providers may request non-covered, unlisted or restricted items using their identifiable HCPCS code. If no HCPCS code exists, providers may use the national miscellaneous code L8499 .
Items approved by this procedure may be manually priced. Please include the appropriate manual pricing documentation with the prior authorization request.
Providers should expect medical necessity reviews using this procedure to take longer than usual.
Claims for items approved using this procedure should also be submitted through NCTracks.
If denied, the provider and beneficiary will be notified, and normal beneficiary appeal rights will apply.
Providers will be notified if the device requested is covered by a different NC Medicaid policy area or waiver program.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:5B:3.2.1
Title: 3.2.1 Specific criteria covered by Medicaid
Section: 3.2.1
Policy: 5B
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched limitation.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover orthotics and prosthetics when the beneficiary meets all the following specific criteria:
they are ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner;
they are medically necessary to maintain or improve a beneficiary's medical, physical or functional level, and appropriate for use in any noninstitutional setting in which normal life activities take place;
a documented face-to-face encounter with the beneficiary and the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner related to the primary reason the beneficiary requires orthotics and prosthetics has occurred no more than six (6) months prior to the initiation of orthotics and prosthetics; and
the beneficiary's need for orthotics and prosthetics is reviewed by the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner at least annually.
Medicaid covers orthotic and prosthetic services when they are medically necessary, and the beneficiary meets the specific coverage requirements for the device.
Orthotic devices are medically necessary when required to correct or prevent skeletal deformities, to support or align movable body parts, or to preserve or improve physical function.
Prosthetic devices are medically necessary as a replacement for all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part. The beneficiary shall require the prosthesis for mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation purposes.
In addition, orthotic and prosthetic devices must be:
a reasonable and medically necessary part of the beneficiary's treatment plan;
consistent with the beneficiary's diagnosis and medical condition, particularly the functional limitations and symptoms exhibited by the beneficiary; and
of high quality, with replacement parts available and obtainable.
Medical doctors (MDs), doctors of osteopathic medicine (DOs), doctors of podiatric medicine (DPMs), physician assistants (PAs) and nurse practitioners (NPs) may provide certain orthotic and prosthetic devices when the devices are part of the beneficiary's current care and treatment. These professionals may provide devices as indicated in the Required Provider Certification column of Attachment B .
To be reimbursed for an orthotic or prosthetic device, the provider shall be enrolled as an appropriate board-certified provider for the specific device. Refer to Attachment B, which includes the Required Professional Certification for Orthotic and Prosthetic Devices.
For specific coverage requirements, refer to Subsection 5.3, Documenting Medical Necessity.

Section: 2.2.1

Content:
42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed practitioner).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services will be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

per_question.question: Is acupuncture listed as a covered treatment anywhere in Clinical Coverage Policy 8C for outpatient behavioral health?
per_question.agent_answer:
No. Acupuncture is not listed as a covered outpatient behavioral health treatment in Clinical Coverage Policy 8C as currently effective April 15, 2025. The policy’s service description lists covered outpatient behavioral health services as psychiatric and comprehensive clinical assessment, medication management, individual, group, and family therapies, psychotherapy for crisis, and psychological testing; for SUD services it also lists SBIRT, but it does not list acupuncture. [Policy 8C § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

For coverage generally, Medicaid covers outpatient behavioral health services under Policy 8C when the beneficiary meets the coverage criteria in Section 3.0, but the covered-service description in Section 1.0 does not include acupuncture. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) [Policy 8C § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

For the not-covered side, Policy 8C says Medicaid does not cover procedures, products, and services related to the policy when the beneficiary does not meet Section 2.0 eligibility, does not meet Section 3.0 criteria, the service duplicates another provider’s service, or the service is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial. [Policy 8C § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) The outpatient behavioral health-specific not-covered list includes sleep therapy for psychiatric disorders and several setting/medical-necessity limitations, but it also does not identify acupuncture as a covered modality anywhere in that section. [Policy 8C § 4.2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

I also checked the amendment history for Policy 8C. The current policy has later revisions effective January 1, 2025 and April 15, 2025, and the April 15, 2025 change notice addressed Section 3.2.2, not the covered-service list in Section 1.0. [Policy 8C Change Notice 2025-04-15](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) [Policy 8C Change Notice 2025-01-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

If you want, I can also check whether acupuncture is covered anywhere else in NC Medicaid outside Policy 8C.

---

*Suggested citations for uncited claims above:*
- [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)
- [8C § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)
